items.title: Show HN: Rat Race (After Dark, 1994), ported from 68k assembly to TypeScript
items.contentSnippet:
Ported to TypeScript from Motorola 68k assembly!
All the rats' behaviors are true to spec: Their distractions (sniffing, turning around, grooming, stopping) are all frame accurate and occur in the same ratios as the original. The artwork and animation speeds were extracted from the old bitmaps and jump instructions and are (as close as I can get) to being frame accurate.

items.title: Show HN: Vork – headless 3D and VFX engine for agents
items.contentSnippet:
I made an agent-native 3d/vfx engine.
Agents are good at making interesting scenes in Blender/Unreal/Nuke/etc. But these tools are fundamentally limited compared to what coding agents are capable of. Many simplifying assumptions are baked into these tools in order to fit human authoring methods.
In vork, agents write the whole scene as code, including their own shaders, materials, cameras and physics, and vork renders it on the GPU. The core API fits in about 2,500 tokens.

items.contentSnippet:
Hello HN, I’m Daniel and I run ZoomHub, a small deep zoom image service.
Most online catalogs look the same: There’s a grid of thumbnails, limited to about 20–50 items, filters that refresh the page when activated, and pagination buttons to go to page 22 of 128.

Hi HN, I’m a reverse engineer, and I’ve seen the same problem repeatedly: people need data, but the path from “I need this” to “my app, agent, or workflow can use it” is messy.
Vibe coders want a working endpoint in minutes. Developers want clean docs, predictable JSON, and no surprise integration work.
